slices.label: Men outside the South
slices.source: 1940 census (April, the first to recode Mexican-origin people as white and to tabulate citizenship for all foreign-born) aged to November 1940; men 21+ outside the eleven Southern states, citizens only, American Indians included as citizens since 1924; Black voters here vote heavily Democratic since 1936; calibrated to certified 1940 returns.

slices.label: Women outside the South
slices.source: 1940 census aged to November 1940, women 21+ outside the South, all enfranchised by the Nineteenth Amendment; turnout from the carried-forward women-to-men ratio, calibrated to each state's 1940 vote.

slices.label: White Southerners
slices.source: 1940 census aged to November 1940, white adults (now including Mexican-origin adults) in the eleven former Confederate states; poll taxes remain in eight (North Carolina, Louisiana and Florida have repealed theirs); calibrated to certified 1940 returns.

slices.label: Black Southerners
slices.source: 1940 census aged to November 1940, Black adults in the eleven former Confederate states; disfranchisement by poll tax, literacy test and the white primary continues, so the shortfall against white turnout is counted as exclusion; the few who vote lean Democratic since 1936.

slices.label: Immigrants not yet citizens
slices.source: 1940 census aged to November 1940, foreign-born white adults who were not naturalized; no state let aliens vote.

runs.summary: Rerun with nothing changed, 1940 comes out as it did: Roosevelt wins, 449–82. The closest state was Michigan, which went to Willkie by 0.3 points. Every one of my 100 reruns reproduces it exactly.
howIGotThis: The numbers: the 1940 census counts and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1940 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.

everyone.summary: 34.4 million more adults vote. Maine, Michigan flip, but Roosevelt still wins, 473–58. The closest call is Indiana, which holds for Willkie by 0.7 points. Willkie wins in 0 of 100 draws.
assumptions: Every adult votes. Non-citizens choose like naturalized citizens of their state and sex; Black Southerners like Black voters outside the South; everyone else as their group did in 1940.
howIGotThis: What changed: Every adult can vote, and turns out.
New voters borrow the behaviour of naturalized citizens of the same state and sex; Black voters outside the South.

south-white.name: Anna Reed
south-white.quote: I suppose I ought to vote tomorrow if I can get through the registration business. The President's done well enough by people like us.
south-white.controlQuote: I suppose I ought to vote tomorrow if I can get through the registration business. The President's done well enough by people like us.

women.name: Ruth Robinson
women.quote: I expect I'll go vote tomorrow. The country's helping those people fighting the aggressor nations, and we need to keep our own strength up. Can't leave it to chance.
women.controlQuote: I expect I'll go vote tomorrow. The country's helping those people fighting the aggressor nations, and we need to keep our own strength up. Can't leave it to chance.

men.name: Ernest Reed
men.quote: The President's got people back to work around here. That matters more than what the other fellow promises. Though I'm not entirely comfortable with him running again.
